results.title: How to de-slop AI output with a custom skill
results.summary: This video introduces a custom skill for AI output quality control, addressing issues like AI slop, factual inaccuracies, and brand misalignment.

data.tldr: The video explains the concept of 'AI slop' – output that is technically correct but doesn't meet quality standards or brand guidelines. The creator, Ben AI, introduces a custom skill designed to de-slop AI output by running it through universal and company-specific checks. This skill helps identify issues like AI writing tells, factual inaccuracies, inconsistencies, and voice misalignment, providing suggestions for improvement. The skill can be downloaded for free and personalized for individual or company use, aiming to ensure AI outputs are consistently high-quality and aligned with brand standards.
keyPoints: AI slop refers to AI-generated content that is technically correct but fails to meet quality standards, brand guidelines, or specific context.
The subjectivity of 'slop' necessitates a standardized de-sloping process, especially in business contexts.
The de-slop skill automates checks for AI writing tells, factual accuracy, consistency, artifacts, readability, voice, company fit, and completeness.
It includes both universal checks and company-specific checks to ensure alignment with brand voice, strategy, and facts.
The skill provides a verdict and suggestions for improvement, helping users refine AI outputs before they are published.
The de-slop skill can be downloaded for free and personalized to fit individual or company needs.
The creator also offers a 'De-Slop Builder' skill to help users create their own personalized de-slop skills.
The video references an a16z article on 'Institutional AI vs Individual AI' which discusses the productivity paradox of AI adoption.

results.title: Every level of a claude code second brain explained
results.summary: This video explains five levels of building a Claude Code second brain, from simple file routing to autonomous agents, focusing on finding the right level for your needs.

data.tldr: This video breaks down five levels of building a Claude Code second brain, from a simple CLAUDE.md router to an always-on autonomous system. The goal is to find the lowest level that solves your pain, rather than forcing a higher level. The levels are: Level 1 (Folder + CLAUDE.md), Level 2 (Curated Wiki), Level 3 (Semantic Search), Level 4 (Knowledge Graph), and Level 5 (Always-on Brain-OS).
keyPoints: Level 1 involves a simple folder structure and CLAUDE.md file for basic routing and information retrieval.
Level 2 builds on Level 1 by creating a curated wiki, asking Claude for an index, and using Smart Connections for auto-memory.
Level 3 utilizes semantic search, allowing for meaning-based searches rather than just keyword matching.
Level 4 involves knowledge graphs, which represent relationships between entities and are useful for complex queries.
Level 5, the 'Always-on Brain-OS' or 'gbrain', is an autonomous system that runs agents and consolidates information without user intervention.
The key is to find the lowest level that solves your specific pain point, rather than forcing a more complex system.
The video provides a framework for building your second brain based on context, connections, capabilities, and cadence.

quotes.text: The goal isn't to climb to level five. It's to find the lowest level that actually solves your pain so you stop re-explaining things and your agent always knows where to look.
Start with the question, not the tech.
Two jobs. One that matters. Saving Finding. Notes IN. Everyone obsesses here. Notes OUT. where it falls apart. The ladder measures one thing: can you find it again?
Complexity climbs as you go up, not cost. Most people land at 1-3.

results.title: Best ever chocolate brownies recipe
results.summary: A super easy brownie recipe yielding 16 squares with a shiny, papery crust after 25 minutes baking at 180C.

steps: Cut 185g unsalted butter into small cubes and tip into a medium bowl. Break 185g dark chocolate into small pieces and drop into the bowl.

Fill a small saucepan about a quarter full with hot water, then sit the bowl on top so it rests on the rim of the pan, not touching the water. Put over a low heat until the butter and chocolate have melted, stirring occasionally to mix them.
Remove the bowl from the pan. Alternatively, cover the bowl loosely with cling film and put in the microwave for 2 minutes on High. Leave the melted mixture to cool to room temperature.
While you wait for the chocolate to cool, position a shelf in the middle of your oven and turn the oven on to 180C/160C fan/gas 4.

Using a shallow 20cm square tin, cut out a square of kitchen foil (or non-stick baking parchment) to line the base. Tip 85g plain flour and 40g cocoa powder into a sieve held over a medium bowl. Tap and shake the sieve so they run through together and you get rid of any lumps.
Chop 50g white chocolate and 50g milk chocolate into chunks on a board.

Break 3 large eggs into a large bowl and tip in 275g golden caster sugar. With an electric mixer on maximum speed, whisk the eggs and sugar. They will look thick and creamy, like a milk shake. This can take 3-8 minutes, depending on how powerful your mixer is. You’ll know it’s ready when the mixture becomes really pale and about double its original volume. Another check is to turn off the mixer, lift out the beaters and wiggle them from side to side. If the mixture that runs off the beaters leaves a trail on the surface of the mixture in the bowl for a second or two, you’re there.

Pour the cooled chocolate mixture over the eggy mousse, then gently fold together with a rubber spatula. Plunge the spatula in at one side, take it underneath and bring it up the opposite side and in again at the middle. Continue going under and over in a figure of eight, moving the bowl round after each folding so you can get at it from all sides, until the two mixtures are one and the colour is a mottled dark brown. The idea is to marry them without knocking out the air, so be as gentle and slow as you like.
Hold the sieve over the bowl of eggy chocolate mixture and resift the cocoa and flour mixture, shaking the sieve from side to side, to cover the top evenly.

Gently fold in this powder using the same figure of eight action as before. The mixture will look dry and dusty at first, and a bit unpromising, but if you keep going very gently and patiently, it will end up looking gungy and fudgy. Stop just before you feel you should, as you don’t want to overdo this mixing.
Finally, stir in the white and milk chocolate chunks until they’re dotted throughout.

Pour the mixture into the prepared tin, scraping every bit out of the bowl with the spatula. Gently ease the mixture into the corners of the tin and paddle the spatula from side to side across the top to level it.

Put in the oven and set your timer for 25 mins. When the buzzer goes, open the oven, pull the shelf out a bit and gently shake the tin. If the brownie wobbles in the middle, it’s not quite done, so slide it back in and bake for another 5 minutes until the top has a shiny, papery crust and the sides are just beginning to come away from the tin. Take out of the oven.

Leave the whole thing in the tin until completely cold, then, if you’re using the brownie tin, lift up the protruding rim slightly and slide the uncut brownie out on its base. If you’re using a normal tin, lift out the brownie with the foil (or parchment). Cut into quarters, then cut each quarter into four squares and finally into triangles.
They’ll keep in an airtight container for a good two weeks and in the freezer for up to a month.
